items.title: Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy
items.feed_description: A technical analysis of three chained zero-day vulnerabilities in Siemens ROX II OT switches that allow privilege escalation and persistent root access. The post Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy appeared first on Unit 42 .
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers, in collaboration with Siemens, discovered three zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-40947, CVE-2025-40948, CVE-2025-40949) in Siemens ROX II OT switches that enable privilege escalation and persistent root access. The vulnerabilities form a chained exploit allowing attackers to compromise industrial control networks. Siemens recommends updating to firmware V2.17.1 to address these issues.
features: CVE-2025-40948: Arbitrary file disclosure via insecure xz utility configuration
CVE-2025-40947: Command injection via flawed feature key validation
CVE-2025-40949: Persistent root code execution via cron table manipulation
Firmware fix: Siemens ROX II V2.17.1 addresses all three vulnerabilities
Palo Alto Networks NGFW with Advanced Threat Prevention provides virtual patching detection
items.why_it_matters: Critical infrastructure operators must urgently patch affected ROX II switches to prevent full system compromise. The chained vulnerabilities demonstrate how OT devices can become attack vectors, emphasizing the need for continuous monitoring and firmware updates in industrial environments.

items.title: AI Security Is Never Finished: Building the Continuous Red Teaming Loop
items.feed_description: Security programs are built around moments of closure: the finding is closed, the control passed, and the release can move forward. AI security refuses to cooperate with that model. A passing test is useful evidence, but only for a specific system, configuration, and moment. Production AI keeps moving. Models change behavior, prompts are revised, retrieval sources are added, agents gain tools, and users introduce unexpected context. Attackers adapt just as quickly. Yesterday’s clean result may not describe tomorrow’s risk. That has been the practical case for continuous AI red teaming. Now, research from the National Institute of Standards and Technology […] The post AI Security Is Never Finished: Building the Continuous Red Teaming Loop appeared first on Check Point Blog .
items.summary: Check Point highlights the limitations of static AI security testing, citing NIST research that proves no finite guardrails can universally protect against adversarial prompts. The company emphasizes continuous red teaming as a necessity for AI security, introducing the AI Defense Plane to integrate discovery, protection, governance, and assurance. This approach addresses evolving AI risks through ongoing testing, runtime protection, and adaptive governance.
features: Continuous adversarial discovery for identifying attack paths
Continuous hardening to refine policies and controls
Operational resilience for limiting exploit impact
AI Defense Plane integrating discovery, protection, governance, and assurance
items.why_it_matters: Endpoint security teams must adopt continuous testing and adaptive defenses to counter evolving AI threats, as static assessments cannot guarantee long-term protection against sophisticated attacks.

items.title: TuxBot v3: Inside an IoT Botnet Framework With LLM-Assisted Development
items.feed_description: TuxBot v3 Evolution, an IoT botnet framework built with LLMs. Read our analysis of its cross-compiled binaries, C2 architecture and bugs. The post TuxBot v3: Inside an IoT Botnet Framework With LLM-Assisted Development appeared first on Unit 42 .
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers uncovered TuxBot v3, a modular IoT botnet framework leveraging LLM-assisted development with cross-architecture compilation, a Go-based C2 server, and DDoS capabilities. The framework includes exploit code for 30+ IoT devices, fallback C2 mechanisms like DGA and P2P gossip, and a production-ready build with potential ties to known botnet ecosystems. Researchers identified critical bugs in LLM-generated code and a XOR key decryption flaw affecting 9 entries in the string table.
features: Cross-compiled C-based bot agent for 17 architectures (ARM, MIPS, x86_64, etc.)
Go-based C2 server with DDoS-for-hire panel and SSH admin interface
Custom exploit VM and Docker-based test infrastructure
1,496 Telnet credential pairs for device compromise
SHA512 DGA, Ed25519-signed P2P gossip fallback C2
XOR key decryption bug affecting 9 string table entries
Dual versioning (3.5.2 installer vs 3.0.0-EVOLUTION-FINAL Docker)
items.why_it_matters: Endpoint security teams must enhance IoT device protection against LLM-assisted botnets using cross-architecture malware and DDoS capabilities. The XOR key bug and incomplete LLM-generated code highlight risks of AI-assisted malware development, requiring updated detection rules and network monitoring for suspicious C2 activity.
